question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an INCORRECT preposition.
I am writing to invite you / to give a presentation / for our Jobs and Careers Conference / for engineering graduates.
option_2: I am writing to invite you
option_3: for our Jobs and Careers Conference
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. for our Jobs and Careers Conference.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The complete sentence reads: "I am writing to invite you to give a presentation for our Jobs and Careers Conference for engineering graduates."

• When we speak of an event, function, or conference at which something takes place, the correct preposition to use is "at", not "for". We say "a presentation at a conference", not "a presentation for a conference".

• Rule — Preposition of place/event: "at" is used to indicate the specific event or venue where an action occurs (at the meeting, at the conference, at the party), while "for" is used to indicate purpose, benefit, or duration, not location of an event.

• The segment should therefore correctly read: "at our Jobs and Careers Conference".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "for engineering graduates" is correct as it stands — "for" correctly indicates the target audience/beneficiary of the conference.

• Option 2: "I am writing to invite you" is correct — "to invite" is the correct infinitive form used with "writing" to state purpose.

• Option 4: "to give a presentation" is correct — "to give" is the correct infinitive complementing "invite you".

NOTE

• Commonly confused prepositions in SSC exams: "at" (specific point/event/time), "in" (enclosed space/larger area/month-year), "on" (surface/day/date).

• Other fixed phrases: "preside at a meeting", "arrive at a conference", "speak at a function" — all use "at", never "for".

question: Select the grammatically correct sentence.
option_3: Ragini plays the guitar with a melody.
option_4: Ragini plays the guitar with melodiousness.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Ragini plays the guitar melodiously.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "plays" in the sentence must be modified by an adverb, not an adjective, since adverbs describe the manner in which an action is performed.

• Rule — Adverbs of Manner: An adverb of manner tells us how an action is done and typically modifies a verb. Most are formed by adding "-ly" to an adjective, e.g., melodious → melodiously.

• In "Ragini plays the guitar melodiously", the adverb "melodiously" correctly modifies the verb "plays", telling us the manner in which she plays.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "melodious" is an adjective, and adjectives cannot be used to modify verbs; only adverbs can.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "with a melody" is an awkward and non-idiomatic prepositional phrase; native usage requires the adverb form "melodiously".

• Option 4 is incorrect because "with melodiousness" unnecessarily converts the adjective into an abstract noun, producing an unnatural and non-standard sentence.

NOTE

• Adjective-to-adverb conversion is a frequently tested SSC grammar area: quick → quickly, careful → carefully, happy → happily, melodious → melodiously.

• Always check whether the word being modified is a verb (needs an adverb) or a noun (needs an adjective).

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four parts. Identify the part that contains an error.
(A) I am hearing / (B) that the heat wave / (C) is going to be / (D) worse this year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. A.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "hear" is a stative verb (a verb of perception/senses) and is generally not used in the continuous (progressive) tense when it refers to receiving information or understanding something, rather than the physical act of hearing at that very moment.

• Rule — Stative Verbs: Verbs like hear, see, know, understand, believe, love, want express states rather than actions and are normally used in the Simple Present, not the Present Continuous, when expressing facts, opinions, or information received.

• Here, the speaker means "I understand/I have been told", so the correct form is the Simple Present: "I hear that the heat wave is going to be worse this year."

• Hence, Part (A) "I am hearing" contains the grammatical error.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Part B — "that the heat wave" is grammatically correct; it is a noun clause correctly introduced by "that".

• Option 2: Part D — "worse this year" is correct; "worse" is the correct comparative form of "bad".

• Option 3: Part C — "is going to be" is correct; it correctly expresses a prediction using the "going to" future construction.

NOTE

• Other common stative verbs that avoid the continuous form in SSC exams: know, believe, understand, prefer, seem, appear, possess, resemble, belong, remember.

• Exception: some stative verbs can take continuous form with a change in meaning (e.g., "I am seeing a doctor" = meeting/consulting, not perceiving).

question: Select the option with the correct use of future tense.
option_1: I hope your health is getting better by next week.
option_2: I hope your health will get better by next week.
option_3: I hope your health have been getting better by next week.
option_4: I hope your health is get better by next week.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. I hope your health will get better by next week.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence expresses a hope/expectation about a future event ("by next week"), which requires the Simple Future Tense.

• Rule — Simple Future Tense: Subject + will/shall + V1 (base form) + Object. Here, "will get" correctly uses the base form "get" after the modal "will".

• The time expression "by next week" confirms that a future action/state is being referred to, which correctly pairs with "will get".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "is getting" is Present Continuous Tense, which describes an action happening now or around now, not a future outcome expected by next week.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "have been getting" is Present Perfect Continuous, and it is also grammatically mismatched with the singular subject "health", which requires "has", not "have".

• Option 4 is incorrect because "is get" is an ungrammatical combination — a be-verb cannot be directly followed by a base-form verb like "get" without "-ing" or "to".

NOTE

• After modals (will, shall, can, may, must), always use the base form (V1) of the verb, never -ing, -s, or the past form.

• Common future-time markers tested by SSC: tomorrow, next week, soon, by the time, in future.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Once upon a time, there was a man (1)____ used to tell the fortunes of people. One day, he was telling the fortune as usual when a man came to him and said, "Somebody (2)____ broken the door of your house and has stolen many valuables. Go home at once!" The fortune teller was (3)______ shocked to hear the news. He could not utter a word out of shock. He just ran to his house as fast as he could. He was in such a hurry that he left all his things behind. Now, one of his customers saw him rushing and (4)_____, "Every day he (5)______ the fortunes of so many people but today he could not see his own future!" The fortune teller felt very embarrassed.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. who.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a relative pronoun that acts as the subject of the verb "used to tell" within the relative clause **"___ used to tell the fortunes of people", referring back to the antecedent "a man"**.

• Rule — Relative Pronouns: "who" is used as a subject relative pronoun for persons; "whom" is used as an object relative pronoun for persons; "whose" shows possession.

• Since the relative pronoun here performs the action of the verb (it tells fortunes), the subject form "who" is required: "a man who used to tell the fortunes of people."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "whose" is incorrect because it indicates possession (e.g., "a man whose house..."), which does not fit here as there is no possessive relationship being described.

• Option 2: "whom" is incorrect because "whom" functions as an object pronoun and cannot serve as the subject of the verb "used to tell".

• Option 3: "by whom" is incorrect because it would require a passive construction (e.g., "a man by whom fortunes were told"), which does not match the active verb structure "used to tell" given here.

NOTE

• Quick check for who vs whom: if the pronoun can be replaced by "he/she" in the clause, use "who"; if it can be replaced by "him/her", use "whom".

• Relative pronouns commonly tested by SSC: who (subject, person), whom (object, person), whose (possession), which (thing), that (person/thing, defining clauses).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Once upon a time, there was a man (1)____ used to tell the fortunes of people. One day, he was telling the fortune as usual when a man came to him and said, "Somebody (2)____ broken the door of your house and has stolen many valuables. Go home at once!" The fortune teller was (3)______ shocked to hear the news. He could not utter a word out of shock. He just ran to his house as fast as he could. He was in such a hurry that he left all his things behind. Now, one of his customers saw him rushing and (4)_____, "Every day he (5)______ the fortunes of so many people but today he could not see his own future!" The fortune teller felt very embarrassed.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. has.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"Somebody ___ broken the door of your house and has stolen many valuables." Both actions (breaking the door and stealing) happened before the present moment of speaking and have present relevance, so the Present Perfect Tense** is required.

• Rule — Present Perfect Tense: Subject + has/have + V3 (past participle). Since "somebody" is an indefinite pronoun that always takes a singular verb, the auxiliary must be "has", not "have".

• Also, for parallel structure, the second verb "has stolen" already uses "has", so the first verb **"___ broken" must match with "has" as well: "has broken ... and has stolen."**

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "shall have" is incorrect because it forms the Future Perfect Tense, which does not fit a past event already reported as completed.

• Option 2: "had" is incorrect because it would form the Past Perfect Tense, which is used only when two past actions are being compared (one before the other); here, only Present Perfect fits, matching "has stolen."

• Option 3: "have" is incorrect because "somebody" is a singular indefinite pronoun and always takes the singular auxiliary "has", not "have."

NOTE

• Indefinite pronouns like somebody, someone, anybody, everybody, nobody are always treated as singular and take singular verbs (has, is, was).

• Present Perfect Tense is commonly used to describe a recently completed action with present relevance, especially in reported speech/dialogue.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Once upon a time, there was a man (1)____ used to tell the fortunes of people. One day, he was telling the fortune as usual when a man came to him and said, "Somebody (2)____ broken the door of your house and has stolen many valuables. Go home at once!" The fortune teller was (3)______ shocked to hear the news. He could not utter a word out of shock. He just ran to his house as fast as he could. He was in such a hurry that he left all his things behind. Now, one of his customers saw him rushing and (4)_____, "Every day he (5)______ the fortunes of so many people but today he could not see his own future!" The fortune teller felt very embarrassed.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. quite.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires an intensifier/adverb of degree to modify the adjective "shocked" in the sentence **"The fortune teller was ___ shocked to hear the news."**

• Rule — Adverbs of Degree: Words like quite, very, extremely, completely are used before adjectives to intensify their meaning. "Quite shocked" is a natural, idiomatic collocation meaning "considerably/thoroughly shocked."

• The other options are grammatically unsuited to modify a single adjective like "shocked" in this structure.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "so less" is incorrect and grammatically meaningless before an adjective like "shocked" — "so" and "less" cannot be combined this way to intensify an adjective.

• Option 2: "so more" is incorrect for the same reason; "so more" is not standard English usage before an adjective.

• Option 3: "many" is incorrect because "many" is used before plural countable nouns, not before an adjective like "shocked."

NOTE

• Common degree adverbs tested by SSC: quite, rather, fairly, extremely, utterly, completely, thoroughly — all used directly before adjectives/adverbs.

• "Quite" can mean "fairly" (with gradable adjectives) or "completely" (with non-gradable/extreme adjectives like "shocked", "amazed", "astonished").

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Once upon a time, there was a man (1)____ used to tell the fortunes of people. One day, he was telling the fortune as usual when a man came to him and said, "Somebody (2)____ broken the door of your house and has stolen many valuables. Go home at once!" The fortune teller was (3)______ shocked to hear the news. He could not utter a word out of shock. He just ran to his house as fast as he could. He was in such a hurry that he left all his things behind. Now, one of his customers saw him rushing and (4)_____, "Every day he (5)______ the fortunes of so many people but today he could not see his own future!" The fortune teller felt very embarrassed.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. commented.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage is narrated in the Simple Past Tense throughout (e.g., "saw him rushing"), so the verb in the blank must also be in the Simple Past Tense to maintain consistency.

• Rule — Sequence/Consistency of Tense: When a narrative is set in the past, all main verbs describing the sequence of past events should remain in the Simple Past Tense unless there is a specific reason (like reported general truths) to shift.

• The sentence reads: **"...one of his customers saw him rushing and ___, 'Every day he tells...'" — since "saw" is past tense, the parallel verb joined by "and" must also be past tense: "commented."**

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "comments" is incorrect because it is Simple Present Tense, which breaks the past-tense narrative sequence.

• Option 3: "commenting" is incorrect because a bare -ing form cannot function as the main verb of a clause without an auxiliary (e.g., "was commenting" would be needed, not "commenting" alone).

• Option 4: "comment" is incorrect because it is the base form and does not agree with the past-tense parallel structure established by "saw."

NOTE

• When two verbs are joined by "and" describing actions by the same subject in a narrative, they must be in the same tense for grammatical parallelism.

• Watch for tense-consistency errors in SSC cloze passages — identify the dominant narrative tense first, then match blanks accordingly.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Once upon a time, there was a man (1)____ used to tell the fortunes of people. One day, he was telling the fortune as usual when a man came to him and said, "Somebody (2)____ broken the door of your house and has stolen many valuables. Go home at once!" The fortune teller was (3)______ shocked to hear the news. He could not utter a word out of shock. He just ran to his house as fast as he could. He was in such a hurry that he left all his things behind. Now, one of his customers saw him rushing and (4)_____, "Every day he (5)______ the fortunes of so many people but today he could not see his own future!" The fortune teller felt very embarrassed.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. tells.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank appears inside the customer's direct speech: **"Every day he ___ the fortunes of so many people but today he could not see his own future!" This describes a habitual, general routine (what the fortune teller does every day), which requires the Simple Present Tense**.

• Rule — Simple Present Tense for Habitual Actions: Subject + V1/V5 (verb + s/es for third person singular). Since the subject "he" is third person singular, the verb must take "-s": "tells."

• The word "Every day" is a clear time marker of habitual action, and the contrast with "today" (past tense "could not see") confirms that the daily routine is expressed in the present tense while the exception is in the past.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "tell" is incorrect because it lacks the "-s" required for the third person singular subject "he" in the Simple Present Tense.

• Option 3: "telling" is incorrect because a bare -ing form cannot stand alone as the main verb without an auxiliary like "is."

• Option 4: "told" is incorrect because it is the Simple Past Tense, which does not fit the habitual, everyday routine being described ("every day he ___").

NOTE

• "Every day/always/usually/often" are classic Simple Present Tense markers signalling habitual action, frequently tested in SSC cloze passages.

• Third person singular subjects (he, she, it, name of one person/thing) always take "-s/-es" in the Simple Present Tense.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Lousy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Pitiful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Lousy" means very bad, poor in quality, or contemptible/pitiable. (घटिया/दयनीय)
◦ Example: The hotel service was absolutely lousy, so we complained to the manager.

• "Pitiful" means deserving or arousing pity because of being poor, inadequate, or in a sorry state, which closely matches the negative, poor-quality sense of "lousy." (दयनीय)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Praiseworthy" (प्रशंसनीय): Deserving praise or admiration — this is the opposite sense of "lousy," not a synonym.

• Option 2: "Moral" (नैतिक): Concerned with principles of right and wrong behaviour — unrelated to the meaning of "lousy."

• Option 3: "Funny" (हास्यास्पद): Causing laughter or amusement — this does not capture the "poor quality/contemptible" sense of "lousy."

NOTE

• Other words meaning poor in quality often tested by SSC: shoddy, inferior, mediocre, wretched, deplorable.

• "Lousy" can also informally mean "feeling ill/unwell" (e.g., "I feel lousy today"), which is another sense worth remembering.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Agile
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Sluggish.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Agile" means able to move quickly and easily; nimble and well-coordinated. (फुर्तीला)
◦ Example: The agile gymnast performed the routine with remarkable ease.

• "Sluggish" means slow-moving, lacking energy or alertness, which is the direct opposite of being agile. (सुस्त)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Active" (सक्रिय): Means energetic and lively — this is a synonym of "agile," not its opposite.

• Option 2: "Apathetic" (उदासीन): Means showing no interest or concern; emotionally indifferent — related to attitude, not physical quickness, so it does not correctly capture the opposite of "agile."

• Option 3: "Energetic" (ऊर्जावान): Means full of energy and enthusiasm — again a synonym, not an antonym, of "agile."

NOTE

• Other antonym pairs with "agile" style words tested by SSC: nimble ↔ clumsy, brisk ↔ lethargic, swift ↔ sluggish.

• Do not confuse "apathetic" (indifferent in attitude) with "sluggish" (slow in movement/response) — SSC often places both as distractors together.

question:
Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the given sentence.
The west Africans have a heritage of produsing sculpture using wax and bronze.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Produsing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Producing" — the present participle of the verb "produce," meaning to make or manufacture something.
◦ Example: The factory is producing sculptures using traditional techniques.

• Spelling key: PRODUC(E) + ING → PRODUCING. The letter "c" is retained from the base word "produce"; there is no "s" in its place.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Sculpture" is correctly spelt — a work of art created by carving or shaping material such as stone, wood, or metal.

• Option 2: "Bronze" is correctly spelt — an alloy of copper and tin.

• Option 3: "Heritage" is correctly spelt — something inherited from the past, such as traditions or cultural practices.

NOTE

• Common spelling confusion: words ending in "-duce" (produce, reduce, induce, deduce) form their -ing forms as producing, reducing, inducing, deducing — the "c" never changes to "s."

• Other frequently misspelt SSC words: maintenance, occurrence, embarrass, questionnaire, accommodate.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the following sentence.
His flight departs in 5:00 pm.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. at.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• When referring to a specific/precise point in time (clock time), the correct preposition to use is "at", not "in."

• Rule — Prepositions of Time: "at" is used for precise times (at 5:00 pm, at noon, at midnight); "in" is used for longer periods (in the morning, in July, in 2024); "on" is used for days and dates (on Monday, on 5th July).

• The correct sentence is: "His flight departs at 5:00 pm."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "of" is incorrect — "of" is used to show possession, origin, or association, not a point in time.

• Option 2: "for" is incorrect — "for" is used to indicate duration (for two hours) or purpose, not a specific clock time.

• Option 4: "from" is incorrect — "from" indicates a starting point (often paired with "to"), not a single precise time of departure.

NOTE

• Remember the time-preposition rule with the mnemonic: AT a precise time, IN a longer period, ON a day/date.

• Common SSC traps: "in the evening" but "at night"; "on Sunday morning" but "in the morning" generally.

question:
Select the option that will most suitably substitute the underlined part of the given sentence.
I gave my best dress to her on condition that she return it the very next day in a clean condition.
option_1: on the condition that she would return
option_2: on the condition that she return
option_4: on the conditions that she had return
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. on the condition that she would return.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The main clause "I gave my best dress to her" is in the Simple Past Tense. When the main clause of a sentence is in the past tense, the subordinate clause describing a future action from that past point of view must use "would" (future-in-the-past), following the Sequence of Tenses.

• Rule — Sequence of Tenses: If the principal clause is in the past tense, the subordinate clause must also generally be in a past form; a future action viewed from a past standpoint is expressed using "would + base verb", not "will" or the bare present form.

• Additionally, the idiomatic phrase takes the definite article: "on the condition that..." is the standard, complete form.

• The corrected sentence: "I gave my best dress to her on the condition that she would return it the very next day in a clean condition."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "she return" (bare present form) does not correctly follow the past-tense sequence required after the past main verb "gave."

• Option 3 is incorrect because it drops the article "the" before "condition," and while "returned" is past tense, it does not correctly convey the future-in-the-past sense ("would return") that the sentence requires.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "conditions" (plural) does not match the singular sense intended, and "had return" is grammatically wrong — "had" must be followed by a past participle ("had returned"), not a base form.

NOTE

• "Would" is used to express a future action or intention as seen from a point in the past — commonly tested in SSC sentence-improvement questions.

• Other future-in-the-past structures: "He said he would come"; "She promised she would help."

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The novel highlights the place of the endangered species in the rainforest.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. plight.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Plight" means a dangerous, difficult, or unfortunate situation. (दुर्दशा)
◦ Example: The documentary drew attention to the plight of endangered species facing habitat loss.

• In the given sentence, the novel is drawing attention to the difficult/threatened situation of endangered species in the rainforest, so "plight" is the word that best conveys this sense — the plain word "place" does not capture this idea of hardship or danger.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "prowess" (कौशल/पराक्रम): Means great skill or expertise, especially in a particular activity — unrelated to a difficult situation.

• Option 2: "position" (स्थिति): Means the location or rank of something — too neutral and does not convey the sense of hardship the sentence requires.

• Option 4: "perspective" (दृष्टिकोण): Means a particular attitude toward or way of viewing something — refers to a viewpoint, not the actual difficult condition of the species.

NOTE

• "Plight" is a frequently tested SSC vocabulary word, often used in the context of poverty, refugees, or endangered species — situations of hardship.

• Similar words: predicament, dilemma, adversity — all denote a difficult situation, but "plight" specifically emphasizes an unfortunate or sorry state.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The boy watched a sci-fi movie in the lieu of playing in the game zone.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. in lieu of playing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "In lieu of" is a fixed idiomatic phrase meaning "instead of" or "in place of." (के बदले में)
◦ Example: She was given a day off in lieu of the overtime she had worked.

• The phrase is always used without "the" — the correct form is "in lieu of", not "in the lieu of." It must also be followed by a gerund (-ing form) when followed by a verb, since it functions like a preposition: "in lieu of playing."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "in lieu of play" is incorrect because "play" (used here as a base/noun form) does not fit as naturally after the prepositional phrase in this context; the gerund "playing" (matching the ongoing activity) is required.

• Option 2: "in lieu off playing" is incorrect due to the misspelling "off" instead of the preposition "of."

• Option 4: "on lieu of playing" is incorrect because the fixed phrase always begins with "in", never "on."

NOTE

• Since prepositions are followed by nouns or gerunds (never a bare infinitive), any verb following "in lieu of" must take the -ing form.

• Similar fixed prepositional phrases tested by SSC: in spite of, in view of, in case of, on account of, by virtue of — all followed by a noun/gerund.

question:
Identify the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the following sentence and select its correct spelling from the given options.
The boy found the project to be a peice of cake because it was incredibly easy.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. piece.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "piece" (as in "a piece of cake", an idiom meaning something very easy to do), not "peice."
◦ Example: The exam was a piece of cake for her since she had prepared thoroughly.

• Spelling key: remember the classic rule "i before e except after c" — since there is no "c" immediately before this sound, "i" comes before "e": P-I-E-C-E.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "incrediblly" is incorrect as a spelling correction here because the word "incredibly" in the original sentence is already spelt correctly (single "l"); doubling the "l" would make it wrong, not right.

• Option 3: "foaund" is incorrect — there is no word "foaund" in English; besides, the original sentence already correctly spells "found."

• Option 4: "praject" is incorrect — this is not a valid spelling of any English word; the original sentence already correctly spells "project."

NOTE

• The "i before e except after c" rule: piece, believe, chief, field (i before e) vs. receive, deceive, ceiling (e before i, after c).

• Exceptions to remember: weird, seize, either, neither, foreign, height — these do not follow the standard rule.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the following sentence.
There is also an increase in juvenile delinquency.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Adult.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Juvenile" means relating to young people; youthful, or immature/childish. (किशोर/नाबालिग)
◦ Example: Juvenile delinquency refers to criminal behaviour committed by young people below the age of majority.

• "Adult" means fully grown and mature, which is the direct opposite of "juvenile" (young/not yet mature). (वयस्क)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Teenage" (किशोरावस्था संबंधी): Refers to the ages of 13–19, a synonym of "juvenile" in the sense of youth, not its opposite.

• Option 3: "Puerile" (बचकाना): Means childish or immature in behaviour — this is actually a synonym of "juvenile" (in its figurative sense), not an antonym.

• Option 4: "Minor" (नाबालिग): Refers to a person who is legally under the age of adulthood — again close in meaning to "juvenile," not its opposite.

NOTE

• "Juvenile" has both a literal sense (young in age) and a figurative sense (childish/immature); its opposite "adult" works for both age and behaviour-related contexts.

• Related word pairs tested by SSC: juvenile ↔ adult, minor ↔ major, youthful ↔ elderly.

question:
Fill in the blank using the correct collocation.
We need to ________ a decision on the housing project tomorrow morning.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. make.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct collocation in English is "make a decision", meaning to choose or decide something after consideration.
◦ Example: The committee will make a decision on the new policy next Monday.

• Rule — Collocations: Certain verbs pair naturally with certain nouns in English by convention rather than logic; "make" collocates with decision, choice, mistake, effort, promise, plan, among others.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "draw" is incorrect — "draw" collocates with words like "conclusion" (draw a conclusion) or "comparison," not "decision."

• Option 3: "build" is incorrect — "build" collocates with words like "relationship," "trust," or "career," not "decision."

• Option 4: "frame" is incorrect — "frame" collocates with words like "question," "policy," or "argument," not "decision."

NOTE

• Other common "make" collocations tested by SSC: make an effort, make a mistake, make a promise, make a difference, make progress.

• Contrasting "do" collocations: do a favour, do homework, do business — SSC often tests make vs. do confusion.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Alluring
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Repulsive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Alluring" means highly attractive or tempting; charming. (आकर्षक)
◦ Example: The alluring aroma of fresh coffee drew customers into the café.

• "Repulsive" means arousing strong dislike or disgust; extremely unattractive, which is the direct opposite of "alluring." (घृणित)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Enticing" (लुभावना): Means attractive and tempting — a synonym of "alluring," not its opposite.

• Option 2: "Glamourous" (चकाचौंध भरा): Means attractively and excitingly stylish — again a synonym rather than an antonym.

• Option 4: "Fascinating" (आकर्षक): Means extremely interesting or attractive — also a synonym, not the opposite, of "alluring."

NOTE

• Words expressing attraction commonly tested together by SSC: alluring, enticing, tempting, captivating, charming, fascinating — all synonyms.

• Their opposites include: repulsive, repugnant, revolting, unappealing, off-putting.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence.
It did not take her very long to ascend to power.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. climb.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Ascend" means to rise or move upward; to climb. (चढ़ना/ऊपर जाना)
◦ Example: She ascended to the position of CEO within just five years.

• "Climb" carries the same essential meaning of rising or moving upward progressively (often step by step), making it the most accurate synonym for "ascend" in the context of rising to a position of power.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "grab" (छीनना): Means to seize suddenly and forcefully — implies abruptness/force, unlike the gradual rising sense of "ascend."

• Option 3: "reach" (पहुँचना): Means to arrive at or attain a point — focuses on the endpoint, not the gradual upward movement that "ascend" specifically conveys.

• Option 4: "arise" (उत्पन्न होना): Means to originate or come into being — refers to emergence, not upward movement, so it does not match "ascend."

NOTE

• "Ascend" and "climb" both emphasize gradual upward movement, whether literal (ascend a mountain) or figurative (ascend to power/a position).

• Its antonym is "descend" (to move downward) — a frequently paired opposite in SSC vocabulary questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined part in the following sentence.
My entire family left me in the lurch when I went to them after I divorced my husband.
option_1: refused to help me in my distress
option_2: blamed only me for my failure
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. refused to help me in my distress.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to leave someone in the lurch" means to abandon or desert a person in a difficult situation, without help, especially when they need it most. (मुसीबत में अकेला छोड़ देना)
◦ Example: When the project deadline was near, my colleague fell ill and left me in the lurch.

• In the given sentence, the family failed to support the speaker when she turned to them in her time of need (after her divorce), which matches the meaning "refused to help me in my distress."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "blamed only me for my failure" — this implies active blame/accusation, which is different from simply abandoning someone without help; the idiom does not specifically mean "blame."

• Option 3: "scorned me for committing mistakes" — this implies contempt or mockery over mistakes, which is not the core meaning of "left in the lurch" (which is about abandonment, not scorn).

• Option 4: "attempted to harass me" — this implies active harassment, whereas the idiom refers to passive abandonment/desertion in a time of need, not active harm.

NOTE

• The idiom originates from a French dice/card game term "lourche," meaning a situation where one is left at a serious disadvantage.

• Similar idioms of abandonment tested by SSC: "to leave someone high and dry," "to turn one's back on someone," "to leave someone in the cold."

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.
Prakash could not make up his mind about what to do with the project.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Decide.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to make up one's mind" means to reach a firm decision; to decide definitely after consideration. (निर्णय लेना/मन बना लेना)
◦ Example: After weighing the pros and cons, she finally made up her mind to accept the job offer.

• In the sentence, Prakash was unable to reach a firm conclusion about the project, which directly corresponds to the meaning "decide."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Abandon" (छोड़ देना): Means to give up or desert something entirely — this is a much stronger and different action than simply failing to decide.

• Option 2: "Think" (सोचना): Means to consider or reflect — this is only part of the decision-making process, not the act of reaching a final decision itself.

• Option 3: "Abide" (पालन करना): Means to accept or act in accordance with a rule or decision — unrelated to the process of deciding.

NOTE

• Related idioms of decision-making tested by SSC: "to be in two minds" (to be undecided/hesitant), "to have second thoughts" (to reconsider a decision), "to sit on the fence" (to avoid taking a side).

• "Make up one's mind" is often contrasted with "change one's mind" (to alter a decision already made).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Resourceful
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Incompetent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Resourceful" means having the ability to find quick, clever ways to overcome difficulties; capable and inventive. (साधन-संपन्न/कुशल)
◦ Example: The resourceful manager found a creative solution to the sudden staff shortage.

• "Incompetent" means lacking the necessary skill or ability to do something successfully, which stands in direct contrast to being capable and resourceful. (अयोग्य)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Ingenious" (प्रतिभाशाली/निपुण): Means clever, original, and inventive — this is a synonym of "resourceful," not its opposite.

• Option 3: "Immaculate" (निष्कलंक/त्रुटिरहित): Means perfectly clean or without any flaws — refers to cleanliness/perfection, not capability, so it is unrelated as an antonym here.

• Option 4: "Impeccable" (त्रुटिहीन): Means faultless or flawless — again refers to being without fault, not to a lack of resourcefulness/capability.

NOTE

• "Resourceful," "ingenious," and "inventive" form a common synonym cluster in SSC vocabulary questions.

• Its antonyms include: incompetent, inept, helpless, unimaginative — all indicating a lack of ability or resourcefulness.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Peculiar
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Strange.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Peculiar" means strange, unusual, or odd; out of the ordinary. (विचित्र/अजीब)
◦ Example: There was a peculiar smell coming from the old library.

• "Strange" carries the same core meaning of being unusual or odd, making it the most accurate synonym for "peculiar."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Revolutionary" (क्रांतिकारी): Means involving or causing a dramatic, wide-reaching change — unrelated to the sense of oddness conveyed by "peculiar."

• Option 3: "Frequent" (बार-बार होने वाला): Means occurring often — this relates to occurrence/repetition, not strangeness, so it is not a synonym.

• Option 4: "Usual" (सामान्य): Means normal or expected — this is actually close to the opposite of "peculiar" (which means unusual/abnormal), not a synonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "peculiar" often tested together: odd, bizarre, curious, eccentric, quirky.

• Its antonyms include: normal, usual, common, ordinary, typical.
